items.prose: A rates desk fits a curve $p(t) = a_0 + a_1t + a_2t^2 + a_3t^3$ in $\mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R})$, with $t$ in years. Its report is the linear map $T : \mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^2$, $T(p) = (p(2), p'(2))$: the level and the slope at two years.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Evaluate $t^3$ at 2, then differentiate and evaluate at 2.

byKey.slope-power: You took the derivative of $t^3$ as $3t$. It is $3t^2$, which is 12 at $t = 2$.
byKey.swapped: Those are the right numbers in the wrong order. $T(p)$ lists the level $p(2)$ first.

explain.text: The level comes first and the slope second. Every basis vector $t^k$ goes to $(2^k, k2^{k-1})$.

parts.question: Using $T(t^3) = (8, 12)$ from part 1, write the matrix of $T$ in the basis $(1, t, t^2, t^3)$ and the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Type it as [[a, b, c, d], [e, f, g, h]].

feedback.generic: Not quite. Column $k$ is the image of the $k$-th basis vector, written in the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

byKey.unevaluated: Your second row holds the coefficients of the derivatives, $0, 1, 2t, 3t^2$, read before setting $t = 2$. At $t = 2$ they are $0, 1, 4, 12$.
byKey.rows-swapped: You put the slopes on top. The first row holds the levels $p(2)$, since $T(p)$ lists the level first.
byKey.carried: Your last column uses $(8, 6)$ for $T(t^3)$. The slope of $t^3$ at 2 is $3 \times 4 = 12$.

explain.text: The matrix is $2 \times 4$: one row per entry of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and one column per basis vector of $\mathcal{P}_3$. Times the coordinates $(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ it gives $T(p)$.

parts.question: Using the matrix from part 2, its columns $(1, 0)$ and $(2, 1)$ are independent, so $\dim \operatorname{im} T = 2$. What is $\dim \ker T$? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: Rank-nullity gives $\dim \mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R}) = \dim \ker T + \dim \operatorname{im} T$, so $4 = \dim \ker T + 2$ and the kernel has dimension 2.

byKey.three: You used 3 for $\dim \mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R})$. Its basis $(1, t, t^2, t^3)$ has 4 vectors.
byKey.all: That is $\dim \mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R})$. The kernel is smaller: $T(1) = (1, 0)$ is not zero.

explain.text: A basis of the kernel is $((t - 2)^2, t(t - 2)^2)$. Both curves have $p(2) = 0$ and $p'(2) = 0$.

parts.question: Using the first two columns of the matrix from part 2, $T(a + bt) = (a + 2b, b)$. Find the polynomial $p$ of degree at most 1 with $T(p) = (5, 3)$. Give it in terms of $t$.

feedback.correct: A line with slope 3 through $(2, 5)$ is $5 + 3(t - 2) = 3t - 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A line $a + bt$ has slope $b$ everywhere, so $b = 3$; then make its value 5 at $t = 2$.

byKey.level-at-zero: Your line has value 5 at $t = 0$. The report reads the level at $t = 2$: $3t + 5$ gives 11 there.
byKey.swapped: You used the level as the slope. The slope must be 3, and the level at $t = 2$ must be 5.

explain.text: Check: $p(2) = 6 - 1 = 5$ and $p'(2) = 3$. The lines form a subspace of dimension 2 on which $T$ is one-to-one, so this line is the only one.

parts.question: Using $p_0 = 3t - 1$ from part 4 and $(t - 2)^2 \in \ker T$ from part 3, every $p_0 + \lambda(t - 2)^2$ also has $T(p) = (5, 3)$. Find the one with $p(0) = 7$. Give it in terms of $t$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $t = 0$ in $3t - 1 + \lambda(t - 2)^2$, solve for $\lambda$, then expand.

byKey.no-p0: You set $4\lambda = 7$ and forgot $p_0(0) = -1$. Then $p(0) = 6$, not 7: $\lambda = 2$.
byKey.shift-constant: You changed the constant of $p_0$. That moves the level: $3t + 7$ has $p(2) = 13$, so $T(p) \ne (5, 3)$.

explain.text: Check: $p(2) = 8 - 10 + 7 = 5$ and $p'(t) = 4t - 5$ gives $p'(2) = 3$. Among curves of degree at most 2 the solutions are $p_0 + \lambda(t - 2)^2$, a line, so one more condition picks one curve.

items.prose: A risk engine maps a position $\mathbf{x}$ in two bond futures to its exposures $T\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$, with $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$. The desk thinks in the basis $\mathcal{B} = (\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2)$, with $\mathbf{b}_1 = (1, 1)$ and $\mathbf{b}_2 = (2, 3)$.

parts.question: $T\mathbf{b}_1 = (3, 3) = 3\mathbf{b}_1$. Find the coordinates $[T\mathbf{b}_2]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of $T\mathbf{b}_2$ in $\mathcal{B}$. Give them as $(a, b)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compute $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{b}_2$, then solve $a\mathbf{b}_1 + b\mathbf{b}_2 = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{b}_2$.

byKey.standard: That is $T\mathbf{b}_2$ in the standard basis. In $\mathcal{B}$ it is $4\mathbf{b}_1 + 2\mathbf{b}_2$.
byKey.swapped: Those are the right numbers in the wrong order. $a$ goes with $\mathbf{b}_1$: $4(1, 1) + 2(2, 3) = (8, 10)$.

explain.text: Check: $4(1, 1) + 2(2, 3) = (8, 10)$. Subtracting the two equations gives $b = 2$ at once.

parts.question: Using $[T\mathbf{b}_1]_{\mathcal{B}} = (3, 0)$ and part 1, write $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}$. Type it as [[a, b], [c, d]].

feedback.generic: Not quite. Column $k$ of $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}$ is the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates of $T\mathbf{b}_k$.

byKey.old-matrix: That is $\mathbf{A}$, the matrix in the standard basis. In $\mathcal{B}$ the columns are $(3, 0)$ and $(4, 2)$.
byKey.rows: You wrote the coordinates as rows. That is the transpose; each one goes down a column.

explain.text: It equals $\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}$ with $\mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. In this basis the matrix is triangular, so its eigenvalues 3 and 2 sit on the diagonal.

parts.question: Using $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}$ from part 2, its determinant is 6, so $T$ is invertible. Find $[T^{-1}]_{\mathcal{B}}$. Type it as [[a, b], [c, d]], with fractions where needed.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal ones and divide by the determinant 6.

byKey.entrywise: You took the reciprocal of each entry. The inverse matrix is not entry by entry: its top-right entry is $-\tfrac{4}{6} = -\tfrac23$.
byKey.sign: You kept the sign of the 4. The inverse negates the off-diagonal entry, so it becomes $-4$, and $-\tfrac{4}{6} = -\tfrac23$.

explain.text: Check: $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \tfrac13 & -\tfrac23 \\ 0 & \tfrac12 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{I}$. The matrix of $T^{-1}$ in a basis is the inverse of the matrix of $T$ in it.

parts.question: The desk wants exposures $(11, 13)$, whose coordinates in $\mathcal{B}$ are $(7, 2)$. Using $[T^{-1}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ from part 3, find the position $T^{-1}(11, 13)$ in standard coordinates. Give it as $(x, y)$.

feedback.correct: $[T^{-1}]_{\mathcal{B}}(7, 2) = (\tfrac73 - \tfrac43, 1) = (1, 1)$. Back in the standard basis that is $\mathbf{b}_1 + \mathbf{b}_2 = (3, 4)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply $[T^{-1}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ by $(7, 2)$, then turn the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates back into a position.

byKey.b-coords: Those are the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates of the position. The position itself is $\mathbf{b}_1 + \mathbf{b}_2 = (3, 4)$.
byKey.applied-a: That is $\mathbf{A}(11, 13)$, the exposure of a position $(11, 13)$. The question asks which position has exposure $(11, 13)$.
byKey.carried-sign: That uses the inverse with $+\tfrac23$ in the corner. With $-\tfrac23$ the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates are $(1, 1)$, giving $(3, 4)$.
byKey.carried-entrywise: That uses the inverse with $\tfrac14$ in the corner. With $-\tfrac23$ the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates are $(1, 1)$, giving $(3, 4)$.

explain.text: Check: $\mathbf{A}(3, 4) = (3 + 8, -3 + 16) = (11, 13)$. The position is 3 of the first future and 4 of the second.

items.prose: A desk writes a forward curve as $p \in \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$, with $x$ in years. Its tool reports $Tp = p - p'$, the curve less its slope. $T$ is a linear map from $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ to itself.

parts.question: Find $T(3x^2 + x)$. Give it in terms of $x$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Differentiate $3x^2 + x$, then subtract the result from $3x^2 + x$.

byKey.power: You took the derivative of $3x^2$ as $3x$. It is $6x$, so the $x$ terms are $x - 6x = -5x$.
byKey.order: That is $p' - p$. The tool reports $p - p'$, the curve less its slope.

explain.text: On the basis, $T(1) = 1$, $T(x) = x - 1$ and $T(x^2) = x^2 - 2x$. $T$ keeps the leading term and adds lower terms, which gives $3x^2 - 5x - 1$ here.

parts.question: Using $T(3x^2 + x) = 3x^2 - 5x - 1$ from part 1, $T$ kept the leading term $3x^2$. Which argument proves $\ker T = \{0\}$?

options.text: $p'$ has lower degree than $p \ne 0$, so $p - p'$ keeps its top term.
$T(1) = 1 \ne 0$, so nothing non-zero is sent to 0.
options.why: You checked one vector. The map $p \mapsto p(0)$ also sends 1 to 1, yet it sends $x$ to 0.
Non-zero images of a basis are not enough. $(a, b) \mapsto (a + b, a + b)$ sends both basis vectors of $\mathbb{R}^2$ to non-zero vectors but kills $(1, -1)$.

options.text: $T$ maps $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ to itself, so its kernel is $\{0\}$.
options.why: A map from a space to itself can still send non-zero vectors to 0. $p \mapsto p'$ maps $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ to itself and sends 1 to 0.

feedback.correct: The leading term of $p$ survives in $p - p'$, because $p'$ has lower degree. So $Tp = 0$ forces $p = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. An argument must cover every non-zero $p$, not only the basis vectors.

explain.text: Take $p = ax^2 + bx + c$ with $Tp = 0$. The $x^2$ term gives $a = 0$, then the $x$ term $b = 0$, then $c = 0$.

parts.question: Using $\ker T = \{0\}$ from part 2, what is $\dim \operatorname{im} T$? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: Rank-nullity gives $3 = \dim \ker T + \dim \operatorname{im} T = 0 + \dim \operatorname{im} T$, so the image has dimension 3.

byKey.dim-two: You took $\dim \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}) = 2$. Its basis $(1, x, x^2)$ has 3 vectors.
byKey.null: That is $\dim \ker T$. The image has the rest of the dimension: $3 - 0 = 3$.

explain.text: The image is a subspace of $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of dimension 3, so it is all of it. $T$ is one-to-one and onto, an isomorphism of $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ with itself.

parts.question: Using part 3, $T$ is invertible, so $Tp = x^2 + 3$ has exactly one solution. Find it. Give it in terms of $x$.

feedback.correct: Try $p = x^2 + bx + c$. Then $p - p' = x^2 + (b - 2)x + (c - b)$, so $b = 2$ and $c = 5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $p = x^2 + bx + c$, work out $p - p'$, and match it with $x^2 + 3$.

byKey.applied-t: That is $T(x^2 + 3)$. The question asks for the $p$ that $T$ sends to $x^2 + 3$, so undo $T$.
byKey.one-step: You added back the slope of $x^2$ only. Then $p - p' = x^2 + 1$; the new $2x$ has slope 2, which needs adding too.

explain.text: Check: $(x^2 + 2x + 5) - (2x + 2) = x^2 + 3$. Here $T^{-1}q = q + q' + q''$, since the third derivative of a quadratic is 0.
